title: You Built Your Career. But Did You Build Your Life? [Part 1 of 2]
summary: In the first of a two-part 'Cherie's masterclass', Cherie teaches Jean and the audience the frameworks from Stanford GSB's Engineering a Remarkable Life, a course by the late professor Joel Peterson, as a tribute to him. Part one covers the first of his three pillars, 'a person to be', through three exercises: writing a two-page family history, mapping personal assets and liabilities, and auditing your values by where you spend time, money and mind share, then using mantras to rewire yourself toward who you want to become.

ideas.idea: People spend enormous effort constructing a career but almost none engineering their life, so a remarkable life must be planned across career, family, relationships and children, not just work.
ideas.detail: Engineering a Remarkable Life was taught at Stanford GSB by Joel Peterson, former chairman of JetBlue, head of one of the largest US commercial real estate investment firms, and a decades-long GSB professor and mentor who recently passed away. Cherie says it is not hyperbolic that the class changed her life and she references it daily.

ideas.idea: A remarkable life rests on three pillars, a person to be, someone to love, and work to do, and like a three-legged stool it collapses if any leg is missing.
ideas.detail: Peterson insisted that whom you marry is one of the most important decisions of your life, unusual for a business school classroom, and even brought his wife Diana to class to answer students' questions. Part one addresses who you are; part two covers love and work.

ideas.idea: Before your job, income or LinkedIn accomplishments, know who you are: your values, where you come from, and what you refuse to compromise on, because you cannot intentionally build a life alone or with someone else otherwise.
ideas.detail: This is the first pillar, 'a person to be', and all the exercises in the episode are information collection about yourself, meant to give an honest, non-judgmental look at what you are working with rather than to pretend you are perfect.

ideas.idea: Write a two-page family history by interviewing parents, aunts, uncles and siblings, because you are where you come from whether or not you like it, and it anchors you instead of floating through the world.
ideas.detail: Peterson shared his own story of grandparents, a father raised on an Iowa corn farm, childhood jobs and relatives in the World Wars. Guiding questions: where did family members grow up, what hardships did they face, why did they make their choices, what values kept getting passed down, what patterns kept repeating. For the sisters, education and hard work were triple-underlined values passed down for socioeconomic mobility.

ideas.idea: Your family history does not define you, but you should not close your eyes to it; tracing beliefs and traditions back to events like a displacement a hundred years ago reveals patterns.
ideas.detail: The hosts acknowledge some people come from troubled histories and the exercise can be uncomfortable; do only the parts you can, since even starting puts you ahead of 99.9% of people who never reflect on it.

ideas.idea: Map your personal assets and liabilities: for each factor in your life (education, network, relationships, career, finances), write the asset side and the liability side.
ideas.detail: Stanford GSB gave Cherie a network and learning (asset) but cost two years out of the workforce and student loans (liability). A family member brings joy and learning but may need financial care. Her tech-only network is a rich asset but undiversified when she needs advice in another sector. Her content career built professional reputation and opportunity but takes a real mental toll.

ideas.idea: The word liability can sound harsh; think of it as responsibility, and the point of the life balance sheet is awareness so you can change habits or decide how to actively live with each factor.
ideas.detail: Cherie says her content-creation liability means she needs to change habits and lifestyle to account for the mental toll; Peterson's aim was never self-judgment but a fair, honest look at your life to optimize it.

ideas.idea: Values audit: what you spend your time, money and mind share on reflects your true values, regardless of what you claim to value.
ideas.detail: Peterson's quote, which Cherie thinks about daily. Check your calendar for meetings, evenings and weekends; check where your money goes; notice where your mind wanders in an Uber or on a commute. Peterson joked that he claimed not to value luxury yet kept accumulating a garage of fancy old cars, so he must value them.

ideas.idea: Track a representative week of your time without judgment, because what you do day to day shapes your habits and your habits shape your life and compound.
ideas.detail: Jean suggests logging a week to discover, for example, that you think of yourself as fitness-focused but only went to the gym once. Cherie calendars everything, even dinner with friends, so for others, simply writing down at the end of the day what you spent time on works. Write three items each for time, money and mind share.

ideas.idea: Use mantras to rewire your operating system: what you think shapes what you say, and what you say shapes your life, so state the reframe of who you want to become and repeat it in moments of pressure.
ideas.detail: Peterson, a self-described reactive, emotional person, adopted the mantra 'I am not my emotions' to say to himself when a meeting got heated. He was a believer in neuroplasticity. His four mantras: I have everything I need; it's not about me; I'm not my emotions; I am grateful.

ideas.idea: Writing mantras at the top of your journal every morning can carry you through a breakup by making you less attached to the outcome and more grounded in yourself.
ideas.detail: During a breakup in business school Cherie wrote Peterson's four mantras daily for about a month; she says the journal looks like a crazy person wrote it, but it genuinely made her feel better and more centered.

ideas.idea: Deep honesty about yourself lets you see where you are today, decide who you want to become, and engineer your internal dialogue to close the gap.
ideas.detail: Jean observes the backward-looking exercises (family history, assets and liabilities) are traditional, but the action item, modulating your emotional state through mantras, is progressive and grounded in psychology; the whole class is about rewiring your operating system.

ideas.idea: Always have a plan for your life, and it is okay that it is written in pencil.
ideas.detail: A Peterson quote Cherie repeats constantly: she always needs a six-month, one-year or five-year plan, but so much changes outside your control that the plan must be erasable.
